whyNot.D: A web inspector examines web page content and requests and does not produce a host-wide assessment report.

126.why: Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE) equals Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) times Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO). With an ARO of 5, a $500 SLE gives $2,500, which does not exceed the $2,500 protection cost, so spending is not justified.

whyNot.B: A $1,000 Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) times an Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO) of 5 is $5,000, which exceeds the $2,500 cost and supports buying protection.
whyNot.C: A $2,000 Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) times an Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO) of 5 is $10,000, far above the $2,500 cost, so protection is justified.
whyNot.D: A $2,500 Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) times an Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO) of 5 is $12,500, far above the $2,500 cost, so protection is justified.

127.why: An application manager, as part of mobile device management, controls which apps can be installed and run on company phones, which fits managers who install their own mobile tools.

whyNot.A: A download manager handles file transfers and does not control which applications are installed on company devices.
whyNot.B: A content manager controls documents and data on the device, not which applications users may install.
whyNot.C: A segmentation manager separates networks or data zones and does not govern installed applications.

128.why: A sponsored guest account ties each non-employee's wireless access to an employee sponsor, which provides individual accountability for visitors during events.

whyNot.A: Shared accounts are used by many people at once, which destroys individual accountability.
whyNot.B: A preshared password is the same for everyone, so activity cannot be traced to a specific person.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits permissions but does not by itself identify or hold individual guests accountable.

129.why: System sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of virtual machines (VMs) that consume cluster resources, which is what the audit found as the cluster nears exhaustion.

whyNot.A: A buffer overflow is a memory-handling flaw in software and does not explain a cluster running out of compute resources.
whyNot.B: End-of-life systems no longer receive vendor support, which is not the same as running out of cluster resources.
whyNot.D: Weak configuration means insecure settings and does not describe too many virtual machines (VMs) exhausting capacity.

130.why: The patch system's own report lists a package with the malicious hash, so the file was already infected when the patch manager downloaded it from the source.

whyNot.A: Corruption after leaving the patch system would give a different hash in the report than the one the patch system recorded, but the recorded hash already matches the malware.
whyNot.C: Application whitelist approval would not explain why the patch system itself holds a file with the known malware hash.
whyNot.D: A logic bomb is code that triggers on a condition; nothing in the output shows that, and the matching hash points to infection at download.

131.why: A symmetric algorithm, such as Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), uses one shared key and is fast, which makes it the right choice for encrypting large amounts of data between two users.

whyNot.B: A hash function produces a fixed-length digest and cannot be reversed, so it cannot encrypt data for transmission.
whyNot.C: A digital signature proves origin and integrity but does not encrypt the data itself.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides meaning without real cryptographic protection and is not a sound way to encrypt data.

132.why: A policy requiring badges to be rekeyed annually is an administrative control, because it is a rule or procedure set by management rather than a physical device or technical mechanism.

whyNot.A: A physical control is the lock, badge reader or barrier itself, while this item is the written policy that governs it.
whyNot.B: A corrective control fixes damage after an incident, but an annual rekeying policy is routine and not a response to an event.
whyNot.C: A technical control is enforced by technology such as software or hardware, whereas this is a management policy.

133.why: Hard-coding the full path of each Dynamic Link Library (DLL) the application calls prevents Windows from searching attacker-controlled directories, which is how DLL hijacking works.

whyNot.A: Setting each application's Dynamic Link Library (DLL) individually does not stop the search-order lookup that attackers abuse.
whyNot.C: Disabling DLL access from the Windows registry would break normal application loading and does not address search-order hijacking.
whyNot.D: Renaming the affected Dynamic Link Libraries (DLLs) does not stop an attacker from planting a file under the new name in a searched location.

134.why: A Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Virtual Private Network (VPN) can run in a bridged, layer 2 mode with certificate-based mutual authentication, which lets client Media Access Control (MAC) addresses be visible across the tunnel.

whyNot.A: Tunnel mode Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) encapsulates layer 3 packets, so client Media Access Control (MAC) addresses are not carried across the tunnel.
whyNot.B: Transport mode Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) protects only the payload of layer 3 packets and does not carry client Media Access Control (MAC) addresses.
whyNot.C: Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) alone provides no encryption or certificate-based mutual authentication, and it is normally paired with Internet Protocol Security (IPsec).

135.why: Input validation (checking and sanitizing user-supplied data against expected format, type, and length) rejects malformed web form data before the application processes it, preventing the compromise.

whyNot.B: A proxy server (an intermediary that forwards requests) filters or caches traffic but does not validate data inside the application's own form handling.
whyNot.C: Stress testing (load testing under extreme conditions) checks capacity and stability, not whether malformed input is handled safely.
whyNot.D: Encoding (converting data into a safe representation for output) mainly protects output contexts and does not reject malformed input at entry.

136.why: Recovery is the incident response phase where systems are restored to normal operation, including rebuilding the OS and applications and restoring user data from backup.

whyNot.B: Eradication (removing the threat, such as malware or compromised accounts) comes before recovery; restoring user files back is no longer removing the cause.
whyNot.C: Containment (isolating affected systems to stop the incident from spreading) happens before eradication and restoration.
whyNot.D: Identification (detecting and confirming that an incident has occurred) is an early phase, not the restoration of data.

137.why: A keylogger records keystrokes, which captures typed URLs, usernames, passwords, and text from documents being edited, and often stores them in a local file for later retrieval.

whyNot.B: A rootkit (malware that hides its presence with elevated privileges) conceals itself but does not by nature log typed credentials and document text.
whyNot.C: A bot (a compromised host controlled remotely, usually as part of a botnet) is used for tasks like DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service), not keystroke capture.
whyNot.D: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) gives an attacker remote control, but the captured typed data in a file points specifically to keylogging.

138.why: In incident response, the team must first identify the scope and source of the active exfiltration so that later containment and eradication target the right connection and systems.

whyNot.B: Eradication and recovery come after containment, so performing them first would skip steps and could destroy evidence while exfiltration continues.
whyNot.C: Disconnecting the server is containment, which follows identification of the source and scope, and doing it first may lose volatile evidence.
whyNot.D: Formatting and restoring the server destroys forensic evidence and skips identification and containment, so it is premature.

139.why: Banner grabbing connects to network services and reads their response banners, which reveal software names and versions that an intruder can then match to known exploits.

whyNot.B: Port scanning finds open ports and running services but does not by itself reliably reveal the specific software versions.
whyNot.C: Packet sniffing captures traffic passing on the network, which is passive and not a targeted technique for inventorying software versions.
whyNot.D: Virus scanning looks for malware on a host and does not inventory software versions across a network.

140.why: The code copies user-supplied input into a 12-byte buffer using strcpy, which does not check length, so longer input overflows the buffer. This is a buffer overflow vulnerability.

whyNot.A: A bad memory pointer involves an invalid or uninitialized pointer being dereferenced, but the pointer here is valid and the problem is the unchecked copy size.
whyNot.C: An integer overflow occurs when arithmetic exceeds the range of an integer type, and no arithmetic is performed in this code.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is a hidden access mechanism deliberately placed in software, and nothing in this code provides such access.

141.why: Adding a Proprietary data type refines the classification scheme so data can be labeled more precisely, letting the security policy apply more appropriate protections. This is better data classification.

whyNot.A: Adding a category does not reduce cost, and finer classification may even add handling expense.
whyNot.B: Classification labels control handling and protection, not how searchable the data is.
whyNot.D: A new data type does not expand the privacy officer's authority; it only changes how data is categorized.

142.why: Accounting (the part of AAA, Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting, that tracks and records user actions) produces logs and audit trails of what users did.

whyNot.B: Authorization determines what an authenticated user is permitted to access, rather than recording what they do.
whyNot.C: Authentication verifies that a user is who they claim to be, and does not log subsequent actions.
whyNot.D: Identification is the user claiming an identity, such as a username, and does not track actions.

143.why: Rogue system detection finds unauthorized or unknown hosts that appear on the network, which matches a scanner that identifies new host systems.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner looks for weaknesses on known hosts, such as missing patches, not for newly appearing unauthorized hosts.
whyNot.B: A network-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors traffic for malicious activity and does not inventory new hosts.
whyNot.D: A configuration compliance scanner checks that systems match a defined security baseline, not whether hosts are new or unauthorized.

144.why: Risk acceptance means knowingly choosing to take no action against a risk, typically because the cost of safeguards outweighs the potential loss, which is what the CIO decided.

whyNot.A: Transference shifts risk to another party, such as through insurance or outsourcing, and nothing was transferred here.
whyNot.B: Avoidance eliminates the risk by stopping the risky activity, but the CIO is keeping the exposure.
whyNot.C: Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact of risk through safeguards, which the CIO declined to implement.

145.why: The findings show users keeping old permissions after changing roles (privilege creep). Regular permission auditing and reviews, along with access recertification, catch and remove stale access.

whyNot.A: Separation of duties splits critical tasks among people, but it would not remove the leftover permissions from earlier roles.
whyNot.B: A DLP (Data Loss Prevention) solution detects or blocks data leaving the organization, and does not fix excessive role-based permissions.
whyNot.C: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules to access, but it would not by itself clean up permissions retained after role changes.

146.why: Adware causes unwanted ads, new toolbars, and browser slowness and crashes, along with high memory use. A new search toolbar is a classic adware sign.

whyNot.A: Man-in-the-browser malware intercepts and alters web transactions, typically for banking fraud, and is not usually marked by new toolbars.
whyNot.B: A spoofer impersonates an identity or address, such as IP (Internet Protocol) or email, and is not malware causing these browser symptoms.
whyNot.C: Spyware secretly gathers user information, but typically without visible toolbars and ads that adware shows.

147.why: XORing every byte with a fixed value like 0xFF is trivially reversible without a secret key, so it only obscures the data. That is obfuscation, not true encryption.

whyNot.A: Hashing is a one-way function that produces a fixed-size digest, whereas this XOR operation is reversible.
whyNot.B: Key exchange securely establishes shared keys between parties, and this operation exchanges nothing.
whyNot.C: Encryption relies on a secret key and a strong algorithm, and a fixed XOR with 0xFF has no key and offers no real security.

148.why: A mantrap is a two-door vestibule that allows only one person through at a time after authentication, preventing tailgating and unauthorized entry at the main entrance.

whyNot.A: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals, such as wireless emissions, and does not control who physically enters.
whyNot.B: An air gap physically isolates a network from other networks, and does not stop people entering through the entrance.
whyNot.D: Bollards stop vehicles from ramming into buildings but do not control pedestrian access through the entrance.

149.why: Retina scans and fingerprint scans are biometric authentication methods (something you are) that rely on the user's physical characteristics.

whyNot.A: A MAC (Media Access Control) address table maps device addresses to switch ports and is not a user authentication factor.
whyNot.D: Two-factor authentication combines two factor types and is not itself a physical characteristic.
whyNot.E: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) distinguishes humans from bots and does not identify a specific user.
whyNot.F: A password string is something you know, not a physical characteristic.

150.why: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based simulation in which key staff walk through a hypothetical service interruption and then update disaster recovery plans based on what they learned.

whyNot.A: A business impact analysis identifies critical functions and the cost of downtime. It does not simulate an interruption or test recovery procedures.
whyNot.B: Continuity of operation is the planning concept for keeping essential functions running. It is not a simulated walkthrough of a hypothetical event.
whyNot.D: Order of restoration is the sequence in which systems are brought back online. It is a plan component, not a simulation exercise.

151.why: Certificate chaining means the server presents the intermediate certificate authority certificate (Geotrust Global CA) along with its own, so browsers can build a trusted path to the root and stop showing the trust error.

whyNot.A: Both portals already use the same wildcard certificate for *company.com. The wildcard itself is not what differs between them.
whyNot.C: A trust model describes how certificate authorities establish trust in general. It is not a fix for a server missing its intermediate certificate.
whyNot.D: An extended validation certificate changes the vetting level of the identity. It does not supply a missing intermediate certificate in the chain.

152.why: Federation lets two separate identity domains trust each other's authentication, so users from Company B can access Company A resources without merging domains.

whyNot.A: Attestation is verifying that a system or claim is genuine, such as hardware integrity. It does not enable cross-domain resource access.
whyNot.C: Single sign-on (SSO) lets a user log in once within a trust boundary. By itself it does not connect two independent domains.
whyNot.D: Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol that normally operates within a realm or domain. It does not by itself bridge unmergeable organizations.

153.why: Locality-based load balancing sends each request to the server closest to the client, which reduces latency and speeds up application performance while multiple servers keep the service redundant.

whyNot.A: Round-robin rotates requests evenly among servers without considering distance or performance, so it does not specifically accelerate network performance.
whyNot.B: Weighted balancing sends more traffic to higher-capacity servers. It addresses capacity differences, not network proximity or speed.
whyNot.C: Least connection sends traffic to the server with the fewest active sessions. It balances load but does not reduce network distance or latency.

154.why: The data owner is the senior person accountable for the data and decides its sensitivity and classification level, so Ann should consult the owner.

whyNot.A: A data steward manages data quality and handling standards day to day. The steward does not make the final classification decision.
whyNot.B: A data custodian implements technical controls such as storage and backups. The custodian applies the classification but does not decide it.
whyNot.C: A user only consumes the data under assigned permissions. Users have no authority to set its classification.

155.why: Single sign-on (SSO) lets employees authenticate once and access multiple internal resources, replacing three separate credential sets and reducing complexity.

whyNot.A: A transitive trust extends trust between domains automatically. It does not combine separate credentials for different internal resources into one login.
whyNot.C: Federation links identities across separate organizations. The resources here are all internal, so federation adds unnecessary complexity.
whyNot.D: A secure token is a device or software that generates or carries authentication data. It does not by itself consolidate multiple credential sets.

156.why: Modifying the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache with false address mappings is ARP poisoning, a form of spoofing in which the attacker impersonates another device's hardware address.

whyNot.A: A replay attack resends previously captured valid traffic. It does not alter the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache.
whyNot.C: DNS (Domain Name System) poisoning corrupts name-to-IP (Internet Protocol) address records, not the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache that maps IP to hardware addresses.
whyNot.D: A client-side attack exploits software on the user's machine, such as a browser flaw. It is not manipulation of the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache.

157.why: After containment (isolating the system and stopping the malicious process), the incident response process moves to eradication and recovery, which includes restoring lost data from a backup.

whyNot.B: Wiping the system is a drastic eradication choice and is not the logical immediate next step when the process was already terminated and data needs recovery.
whyNot.C: Documenting lessons learned is the final phase of incident response, performed after recovery is complete.
whyNot.D: Determining the scope of impact is part of identification and analysis, which normally occurs before or during containment, not after it.

158.why: An intrusive non-credentialed scan actively sends exploit-like probes without logon access, which can crash fragile services or systems and cause an outage.

whyNot.A: A non-intrusive credentialed scan only reads configuration and patch data using a valid account, so it rarely disrupts systems.
whyNot.B: A non-intrusive non-credentialed scan passively observes and identifies services without sending harmful probes, so it is unlikely to cause an outage.
whyNot.C: An intrusive credentialed scan can disrupt systems, but the non-credentialed intrusive scan is the more likely cause because it relies on blind exploit-style probing.

159.why: A captive portal on the open guest network can log valid email addresses before granting Internet access, and WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) Enterprise uses 802.1X authentication, the most secure method for staff.

whyNot.A: WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) is a weak PIN-based feature vulnerable to brute force, so it is not the most secure staff authentication.
whyNot.B: A captive portal is not the most secure way to authenticate staff, and guests are supposed to use an open network, not WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access).
whyNot.C: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) is broken and obsolete, and a captive portal does not give staff the most secure authentication.

160.why: A network-based intrusion prevention system (NIPS) can block worm traffic and scanning behavior at the network level and, with behavioral or anomaly detection, can stop zero-day attacks as well.

whyNot.A: A host-based firewall must be configured on each host and does not stop all worm traffic or detect unknown zero-day exploit patterns.
whyNot.B: An enterprise patch management system fixes known vulnerabilities such as the old SMB (Server Message Block) flaw but cannot protect against zero-day vulnerabilities.
whyNot.D: Application blacklisting blocks known bad programs, so it will not catch unknown zero-day attacks or stop network spread of the worm.
whyNot.E: File integrity checking detects changes to files after the fact. It neither eradicates the worm nor prevents future zero-day attacks.

161.why: Sandboxing runs an application in an isolated environment that exposes only the operating system resources it needs, limiting the damage if the application is compromised.

whyNot.A: A staging environment is a pre-production copy used for testing before release. It does not restrict an application's operating system access.
whyNot.C: A secure baseline is a standard hardened configuration. It does not isolate individual applications from operating system resources.
whyNot.D: A trusted operating system enforces mandatory access controls at the system level. It is not a deployment concept for limiting what one application can reach.

162.why: A procedure is a detailed, step-by-step set of instructions for carrying out a specific task, unlike a policy, which states high-level intent.

whyNot.A: A high-level statement of company position on a topic describes a policy, not a procedure.
whyNot.B: Setting a minimum expected baseline of behavior describes a standard or baseline, not a procedure.
whyNot.D: Describing adverse actions for violations describes the enforcement or sanctions portion of a policy, not a procedure.

163.why: The log shows traffic to multicast address 239.255.255.255 on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 1900 being dropped on Ann's own system, which points to the host-based firewall on her desktop blocking it.

whyNot.A: A web application firewall (WAF) protects web servers from attacks like injection. It would not log dropped multicast traffic from Ann's desktop.
whyNot.B: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) monitors and blocks sensitive data leaving the organization. It does not produce this kind of dropped-packet log.
whyNot.D: A UTM (Unified Threat Management) appliance sits on the network, not on Ann's system, and the log comes from her machine.
whyNot.E: A network-based firewall would log on the network device, but this log was taken from Ann's own system.

164.why: A gray box test gives the tester partial knowledge, such as password hashes, before the test begins, falling between black box (none) and white box (full).

whyNot.A: A black box test gives the tester no prior information about the target, not even password hashes.
whyNot.C: A credentialed test uses valid logon accounts, usually for scanning, rather than only password hashes.
whyNot.D: A white box test gives the tester full knowledge, such as source code, diagrams, and credentials, which is more than just password hashes.

165.why: Insiders already have legitimate access, system knowledge, and trust, so they can cause the most damage to an organization. This is the insider threat concept.

whyNot.A: Competitors may be well funded but usually lack internal knowledge and legitimate access to the organization's systems.
whyNot.C: Hacktivists (activist hackers) are motivated by ideology and typically use public attacks like defacement, with limited inside knowledge.
whyNot.D: Script kiddies (unskilled attackers) run prewritten tools and lack the knowledge to cause the most serious harm.

166.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) is published by the certificate authority and lists revoked certificates, so checking it shows whether a certificate is still valid.

whyNot.A: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is the overall framework for managing certificates, not the specific tool for checking one certificate's validity.
whyNot.C: A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) is submitted to a certificate authority to request a certificate, not to validate an existing one.
whyNot.D: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) encrypts and authenticates IP traffic and does not check certificate validity.

167.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) equals SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) multiplied by ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence), so both values must be calculated.

whyNot.B: ROI (Return on Investment) measures the financial benefit of a purchase or control and is not part of the ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) formula.
whyNot.C: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines acceptable data loss in time and is a business continuity measure, not an ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) input.
whyNot.E: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines how quickly a system must be restored and is not used to calculate ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy).

168.why: An account expiration strategy automatically disables temporary and contractor accounts at the end of their engagement, preventing lingering access to trade secrets. This is account lifecycle management.

170.why: Ransomware makes files unavailable, often by encrypting or removing them, and demands payment to restore them. The unknown party requesting funds matches this attack.

172.why: Encrypted email attachments depend on proper authentication and key or certificate exchange. If Ann cannot authenticate or lacks the correct key, the encrypted attachment will not be delivered while headers still arrive.

173.why: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) enforces access using data classification labels and user clearances set by the system, which matches the labeled data described.

whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides meaning by making data harder to read but is not true encryption and provides weak protection.

whyNot.A: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, but this script only deletes files and makes no ransom demand.

whyNot.D: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users, but this is a conditional destructive script.

178.why: Redundancy across network devices and services removes single points of failure and provides capacity and resilience against DoS (Denial of Service) attacks, covering both the application session limit and the router bandwidth limit.

whyNot.A: A SYN (Synchronize) flood mainly exhausts connection resources rather than bandwidth, since SYN packets are small.
whyNot.B: The firewall is not the main target of a SYN (Synchronize) flood, and the described effect concerns the server's connection state.
whyNot.C: SYN (Synchronize) packets are not fragmented, so there is no reassembly of fragments that would crash the server.

180.why: Rapid elasticity lets a virtual environment automatically scale resources up under heavy load, so a flood of traffic is absorbed and a Denial of Service (DoS) attack is less likely to exhaust the server.

whyNot.A: Elasticity adds capacity, not confidentiality controls, so it does not stop data confidentiality breaches.
whyNot.B: A virtual machine (VM) escape exploits hypervisor flaws, and scaling resources does nothing to prevent that.
whyNot.C: Redundancy comes from failover and duplicate systems; elasticity adjusts capacity but does not by itself provide redundant copies.

181.why: A user first claims an identity (identification), then proves it, such as with a password (authentication), and only then is granted permissions (authorization).

whyNot.B: Authorization cannot come before authentication, because permissions are only granted after the identity is verified.
whyNot.C: Authentication cannot come before identification, because there must be a claimed identity to verify.
whyNot.D: Authentication cannot come before identification, because there must be a claimed identity to verify.

183.why: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals from leaving or entering the premises, so wireless transmissions cannot be intercepted by unauthorized people outside the building.

whyNot.A: An air gap isolates a network from others, but it does not work for a wireless network that must transmit purchases to a billing system.
whyNot.B: Infrared detection senses heat or motion and does not stop radio signals from leaking outside the premises.
whyNot.D: Protected distribution systems secure physical cabling, not wireless radio transmissions.

184.why: Joe broke company policy by using an untrusted public wireless network without a Virtual Private Network (VPN) to send confidential email, which exposed the messages to interception.

whyNot.B: Nobody tricked Joe into acting; he chose to use the airport network himself, so this is not social engineering.

whyNot.D: A zero-day attack exploits an unknown software flaw, and nothing here suggests one was used.

whyNot.A: Phishing is a deceptive electronic message such as email, while this attack happened by phone call, which would be vishing.
whyNot.B: Shoulder surfing means watching someone enter sensitive information, and the caller is not observing anyone.
whyNot.D: Dumpster diving means searching discarded materials for information, which did not happen here.

186.why: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) encrypts the message content itself, and SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts mail in transit, so an insider sniffing the network would not read plain text.

whyNot.A: Secure IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) protects only client mailbox retrieval traffic, not message-level confidentiality or server-to-server mail relay.
whyNot.B: DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) validates DNS records and does not encrypt email content.
whyNot.E: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) protects web traffic and does not secure email transported by mail protocols.

187.why: SSO (single sign-on) lets a user authenticate once with one set of credentials for multiple applications, and federation extends that shared login across separate systems or organizations without synchronizing credentials.

whyNot.A: Multifactor authentication adds more verification factors but does not let one credential set work across multiple applications.
whyNot.C: Biometrics is an authentication factor based on physical traits and does not unify credentials across applications.
whyNot.D: PKI (public key infrastructure) manages certificates and keys and does not provide a shared username and password login.

188.why: The auditor should report the exposed Personally Identifiable Information (PII) to the human resources manager, who owns the process and can correct the privacy policy violation.

whyNot.A: Flipping documents face down only hides them temporarily and leaves the underlying policy violation unaddressed.
whyNot.B: Shredding another department's documents is outside an auditor's authority and destroys records the owner may still need.
whyNot.C: A cover sheet does not protect Personally Identifiable Information (PII), and returning documents to an open printer leaves them exposed.

189.why: Gait analysis identifies a person by how they walk, which is a behavior, so it falls under something you do.

whyNot.A: Somewhere you are refers to location, such as geolocation or an Internet Protocol (IP) address, and not to walking behavior.
whyNot.B: Something you are covers physical traits such as fingerprints, while gait is a learned behavior and not a fixed physical trait.
whyNot.D: Something you know refers to secrets like passwords or PINs (personal identification numbers), and gait is not knowledge.

whyNot.D: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures reliability of repairable systems and is not used to calculate Single Loss Expectancy.
whyNot.E: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) measures the expected life of non-repairable items and is not used to calculate Single Loss Expectancy.
whyNot.F: TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) measures lifetime cost of an asset and is not used to calculate Single Loss Expectancy.

191.why: Stratum 0 devices are the authoritative time sources such as atomic clocks or Global Positioning System (GPS) receivers, and keeping them internal avoids relying on external Network Time Protocol (NTP) sources that could be spoofed or manipulated.

whyNot.A: External Stratum 0 sources are reached over untrusted networks, which exposes the Network Time Protocol (NTP) traffic to tampering and spoofing.
whyNot.C: External Stratum 1 servers are outside the organization's control, so they are less secure than an internal time source.
whyNot.D: External Stratum 1 servers are outside the organization's control, so they are less secure than an internal time source.

192.why: Both parties must first agree on the encryption method, meaning the algorithm to use, before they can exchange the shared secret key for symmetric encryption.

whyNot.A: The key exchange happens after the algorithm is chosen, since the key must suit the agreed method.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures provide integrity and non-repudiation, and they are not required before symmetric encryption starts.
whyNot.D: Digital certificates are used with asymmetric cryptography and are not a prerequisite for choosing a symmetric method.

193.why: A digitally signed email proves who sent it and cannot later be denied by the sender, which is non-repudiation.

whyNot.A: Accessing another department's file shares is an access control issue and does not prove who performed an action.
whyNot.B: Using another user's credentials defeats accountability, which is the opposite of non-repudiation.
whyNot.D: Making unauthorized registry changes is a malicious or policy-violating act and does not provide proof of origin.

194.why: Dates of birth, addresses, and phone numbers are Personally Identifiable Information (PII), so the officer would consult the PII portion of the policy to decide whether a breach occurred.

whyNot.A: Public data is meant for open release, and client personal details are not public information.
whyNot.B: Private is a general data classification label and is not the policy section covering personally identifying client details.
whyNot.C: PHI (Protected Health Information) concerns health records, and none were mentioned in the folder.

195.why: DHE (Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) is an asymmetric key exchange that generates a new, separate key pair for every session, which provides forward secrecy.

whyNot.A: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) normally uses a long-term key pair, so it does not generate a new key every time it runs.
whyNot.B: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) creates digital signatures with a long-term key pair and does not generate a new key per run.
whyNot.D: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) is a symmetric integrity function that uses a shared secret key, not an asymmetric function.
whyNot.E: PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) stretches a password into a key and is not an asymmetric function.

196.why: MFA (Multifactor Authentication) requires two different factor categories. A strong password is something you know and a fingerprint is something you are.

whyNot.A: A hardware token and a smart card are both something you have, so this is only one factor category.

whyNot.B: A .pfx (Personal Information Exchange) extension only describes the file format and does not affect whether clients trust the certificate.

whyNot.B: Password length sets a minimum size, but users can still choose a long, weak, or previously used password.

whyNot.E: Password lockout limits failed login attempts and does not control which passwords users choose or reuse.

whyNot.A: Elliptic curve is one specific asymmetric algorithm family, not the general encryption method PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) uses.

whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides or scrambles data without strong cryptography and does not securely protect keys.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit login hours, but the campus closure would not stop a user whose account was still active remotely.

whyNot.D: Decreased boot time is a performance matter and is not a security benefit.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and its main symptom is locked data rather than off-hours outside communication.
whyNot.C: Polymorphic malware changes its code to evade antivirus detection, which describes evasion and not external communication.
whyNot.D: An armored virus uses techniques to resist analysis and reverse engineering, which does not explain external communication.

whyNot.D: ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) alone does not specify tunnel mode, so original headers may remain exposed.

whyNot.C: A backdoor gives an attacker remote access, but it does not by itself record typed conversations into text files.

whyNot.D: Strong ACLs (Access Control Lists) restrict access to resources but do not stop a program the user runs from executing.

whyNot.B: A bot connects to a command and control server and awaits orders, which is different from self-propagating scanning behavior.
whyNot.C: A logic bomb activates on a specific time or condition and does not generate spreading network traffic.

225.why: Banner grabbing connects to a service and reads the identifying greeting it returns. NMAP (Network Mapper) with version detection, Netcat (NC), and Telnet can each open a connection to a port and show the Apache banner.

whyNot.A: Arp (Address Resolution Protocol) shows or edits the table mapping IP (Internet Protocol) addresses to MAC (Media Access Control) addresses, so it cannot read a service banner.
whyNot.B: Tracert (Trace Route) maps the router hops to a destination and does not connect to a service port to read its banner.
whyNot.F: Grep (Global Regular Expression Print) only searches text for patterns and makes no network connection to the web server.
whyNot.G: Nslookup (Name Server Lookup) queries DNS (Domain Name System) for name and address records and does not return a service banner.
whyNot.H: Netstat (Network Statistics) lists the local host's connections and listening ports and does not probe a remote server for banners.
